title: The Nine Hundred: Pico, the Untitled Oration, and the Kabbalah Carried into Latin
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Mirandola, birth in the castle of the Pico
stops.date_confidence: attested; both principal sources agree on the day
stops.campa: In the castle at Mirandola, a small Emilian lordship held between Modena and the Po, Giulia Boiardo bears Gianfrancesco I Pico a youngest son, and they name him Giovanni. The house is minor as Italian houses go, a princedom of Mirandola and a lordship of Concordia kept against larger neighbors, but the mother's line is lettered: she is aunt to Matteo Maria Boiardo, who is writing the Orlando Innamorato in these same years. The title will pass out of Giovanni's hands within thirty years. The memory his contemporaries call prodigious will not.
suggested_refs: The Castello dei Pico at Mirandola, birthplace and family seat
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Mirandola, the boy made apostolic protonotary
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unknown, and no naming document was reachable
stops.campa: He is raised at the court under his mother's direction, groomed for the Church, and remembered afterward for a memory that swallowed whole texts at a single reading. At about ten he is named an apostolic protonotary, a papal honor that no reachable document explains and that his family's influence plainly bought. The office commits him to nothing and opens every library in Latin Christendom to him. Fourteen years later the same papacy will print a bull against his book and send officers across France to bring him in.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Comune of Mirandola, built 1468, which holds portraits of the Pico family

stops.name: Bologna, canon law and the arid page
stops.date_confidence: attested to c.1477, age fourteen, per the Stanford Encyclopedia; month unknown
stops.campa: At fourteen he enrolls at Bologna to read canon law, the training a protonotary is supposed to have. The subject is a machinery of precedent and he finds nothing in it he wants. Within two years he is gone. What he takes from Bologna is not the law but the shape of the disputation, the scholastic habit of setting a thesis down bare and defending it against all comers, which he will one day scale to nine hundred propositions and carry to Rome. Bologna will print his collected works nineteen years later, and he will be dead.
suggested_refs: The medieval studium of Bologna, seat of canon law
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Ferrara, the Este court and a friar heard in passing
stops.date_confidence: the Stanford Encyclopedia puts the move within two years of the 1477 enrolment, giving c.1479; English Wikipedia gives c.1480, the outer bound of the same window. Contradiction flagged, not resolved. Month unknown
stops.campa: He leaves the law for philosophy and comes to the Este court, a humanist capital with a duke who pays for Greek. Here, some accounts hold, he first sees Girolamo Savonarola, a young Ferrarese friar with no reputation yet and no pulpit worth the name. Nothing passes between them. Fifteen years later that friar will preach the funeral oration over his body in Florence, and the philosopher will be buried in a Dominican habit he had asked for at the end.
suggested_refs: The Este court at Ferrara in the 1470s, and the Ferrarese convent that formed Savonarola
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Padua, Aristotle in the Averroist school
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1480-1482 span; month unknown
stops.campa: At Padua the Aristotle taught is the Aristotle of the Arabic commentators, read through Averroes, a philosophy the Florentine Platonists regard as the enemy. He takes it seriously and will still be defending it years later in Florence, where it is not welcome. The conviction that hardens here is the one he never drops: Aristotle and Plato quarrel in words and agree in substance, and the quarrel is a failure of readers. He will set it down as a thesis in Rome and be told by a papal commission that certain things are not for setting down.
stops.quote: If vegetative, he will become a plant; if sensual, he will become brutish; if rational, he will reveal himself a heavenly being; if intellectual, he will be an angel and the son of God.
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, English translation hosted at bactra.org/Mirandola/ (composed 1486)
suggested_refs: Palazzo Bo, historic seat of the University of Padua
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Padua, Hebrew and Arabic under Elia del Medigo
stops.date_confidence: the languages are attested across the whole 1480-1482 Padua period; this single year is a placement within that span and not a source date. The research pool's assignment of Aramaic to del Medigo in 1482 is an error and is corrected to Mithridates in 1486
stops.campa: Elia del Medigo, a Jewish Averroist of Candia, teaches him and takes his money and begins him in Hebrew and Arabic. No Latin philosopher of the century has done this deliberately. The languages are not ornament. He means to read the Jews and the Arabs in their own words, and to show that every tradition says one thing under a different grammar. Del Medigo will translate for him and will later warn him that the Kabbalah he is buying is not what he has been told it is.
suggested_refs: The Latin translations Elia del Medigo made for Pico from the Hebrew Averroes
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Venice, in del Medigo's circle
stops.date_confidence: tradition only. The research pool states this is not confirmed in either Wikipedia or Britannica and that no itinerary survives; the month and day are placements with no evidentiary value
stops.campa: Tradition puts him in Venice during the Padua years, in his teacher's circle, among the Hebrew presses and the Greek exiles and the manuscript brokers who supply both. No itinerary survives and no letter fixes a date. What the city holds for him is stock: codices in three alphabets, sold to a young man with a princely allowance and no interest in anything else. The books he assembles in these years will be catalogued after his death as one of the great private libraries of Italy.
suggested_refs: The Hebrew and Greek book trade of Venice in the 1480s
sources: General biographical tradition, recorded in the research pool as not independently confirmed

stops.name: Padua, leaving for Florentine Platonism
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month unknown
stops.campa: He leaves Padua at nineteen with Aristotle in his hands and Plato pulling at him from the south. Marsilio Ficino has been turning the whole Platonic corpus into Latin at Lorenzo de' Medici's expense, and the translation is remaking what Italy thinks philosophy is. Pico intends neither to choose between the schools nor to referee them. He intends to prove that the choice was never necessary. That is a larger ambition than either school has, and it needs more languages than either school reads.
suggested_refs: Ficino's Latin Plato, completed at Florence in these years
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, entering Lorenzo's circle
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1484; the day is unknown. The research pool also carried a duplicate of this meeting dated 1480, which is wrong by four years and is not followed
stops.campa: He arrives at the Palazzo Medici in November and the circle opens to him at once: Lorenzo de' Medici, Marsilio Ficino, Angelo Poliziano, Girolamo Benivieni. Ficino will remember that on the very day this young man came to Florence he himself finished his Plato, and will decline to treat the coincidence as one. Pico is twenty-one and has already corresponded his way into a reputation. Poliziano and Benivieni become his friends for life, which in his case means ten years, and both will be buried beside him.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Medici on the Via Larga, seat of Lorenzo's household and its scholars
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Paris, the schoolmen and the nine hundred begun
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1485-1486; month unknown. The letter to Ermolao Barbaro is dated 1485 by the Stanford Encyclopedia and is carried here as reconstruction, no edition of it having been consulted
stops.campa: He goes north to the greatest school of scholastic theology in Europe and puts himself through its machinery, the nominalists against the realists, argument cut to the bone and defended in public. It is the technique he needs. In Paris he begins assembling the propositions, drawn from Latins, Greeks, Hebrews, Arabs, Chaldeans and the Kabbalists, that he means to defend against all Europe at once. He also writes to Ermolao Barbaro defending the schoolmen's ugly Latin against the humanists who despise it.
stops.quote: Let a holy ambition enter into our souls; let us not be content with mediocrity
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, trans. Richard Hooker, Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University (composed 1486)
suggested_refs: The letter to Ermolao Barbaro on philosophical Latin, 1485
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'
Wikipedia (EN), 'Oration on the Dignity of Man'

stops.name: Florence, back among the humanists
stops.date_confidence: attested to spring 1486; the month is a placement within that season
stops.campa: He returns from Paris in the spring and resumes his place among Lorenzo's men, the theses growing in his baggage. He is twenty-three, rich, titled, fluent in more languages than anyone he speaks to, and by every account beautiful, a thing his biographers mention as often as his memory. Poliziano and Ficino work beside him. Eighteen months from this spring he will be an arrested heretic in a French fortress, with his book burning across Italy and a papal warrant on the roads behind him.
suggested_refs: The Florentine humanist circle of 1486: Ficino, Poliziano, Benivieni

segments.name: Arezzo, and the Kabbalah at Fratta

stops.name: Arezzo, the abduction of Margherita
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1486 by the Italian record and by the research pool's geography lens; the pool's chronology gave 1485 and contradicted its own geography, and is not followed. Day unknown
stops.campa: In May he attempts to carry off Margherita, wife of Giuliano Mariotto de' Medici, a tax official of Arezzo, and the attempt goes wrong in the street. He is wounded. Armed men come out of the town after him. It is the episode his biographers have kept rearranging, or redating, so that it will fit the philosopher of the Oration. The Italian sources put it plainly and without embarrassment: at Arezzo in 1486 he had a love misadventure over a certain Margherita.
suggested_refs: Italian Wikipedia's account of the Arezzo affair of May 1486

stops.name: The road out of Arezzo, taken and released
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Britannica's account does not fix the site of the capture, and no source consulted names the place of release; the day here is a placement with no evidentiary value
stops.campa: He is run down on the road with the woman, one of his companions killed in the pursuit, and held under guard. What frees him is not law but patronage: Lorenzo de' Medici writes, and Lorenzo's word carries in Tuscany the way an army carries elsewhere. The same protection will be spent on him again two years from now, on a prisoner of the Church held in France. Twice the Medici stand between Pico and a cell. He outlives the Medici who does it by two and a half years.
suggested_refs: The Arezzo-Siena road, where Britannica's account places the pursuit
sources: General biographical tradition surrounding the Arezzo affair

stops.name: Perugia, convalescence and Flavius Mithridates
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1486; the month is a placement. The research pool's chronology dated this 1485 and named Yohanan Alemanno as a convert met here, both errors: the documented figure at Perugia and Fratta is Mithridates
stops.campa: He recovers near Perugia, and there falls in with Flavius Mithridates, a Sicilian Jew converted to Christianity, a documented forger, and a translator of Hebrew and Aramaic mystical texts who works for money. Mithridates instructs him in Aramaic and begins turning the Kabbalah into Latin for him, thousands of pages of it, some of it doctored where the translator judged a Christian reader would want doctoring. Yohanan Alemanno is also named among his teachers in Kabbalah, without place or date.
suggested_refs: The Latin Kabbalah corpus translated for Pico by Flavius Mithridates, 1486

stops.name: Fratta, the Kabbalah rendered into Latin
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1486; the month is a placement. The town has been called Umbertide since 1863
stops.campa: He withdraws to a house at Fratta in the Umbrian hills, and Mithridates lives there with him, translating. Out of this summer comes the claim he will be condemned for: that the secret Jewish tradition, read correctly, proves the Christian doctrines it was supposed to deny, and that no science better confirms the divinity of Christ than magic and the Kabbalah. He is about to say this in Rome, in print, and invite the whole of Europe to come and refute him.
stops.quote: This creature, man, whom Asclepius the Athenian, by reason of this very mutability, this nature capable of transforming itself, quite rightly said was symbolized in the mysteries by the figure of Proteus.
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, English translation hosted at bactra.org/Mirandola/ (composed 1486)
suggested_refs: The villa at Fratta, now Umbertide, where the Kabbalistic translations were made

stops.name: Rome, arriving with nine hundred propositions
stops.date_confidence: attested to autumn 1486; the month is a placement within that season
stops.campa: He comes to Rome in the autumn to stage the largest disputation ever proposed by one man: nine hundred conclusions drawn from Latins, Greeks, Arabs, Hebrews, from Hermes and Zoroaster and the Kabbalists, defended by a twenty-three-year-old against any scholar in Europe willing to come and argue. He offers to pay the travel of anyone who does. The Curia sits a mile from his lodging. Giordano Bruno will be brought before that same Curia a century later and will not be let go.
stops.quote: THE CONCLUSIONS will not be disputed until after the Epiphany. In the meantime they will be published in all Italian universities.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the announcement appended to the 900 Theses, 1486; surfaced via a general Wikipedia query and not verified against a critical edition of the Conclusiones
suggested_refs: Pico's public offer to fund the travel of any scholar who would dispute the nine hundred
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'Oration on the Dignity of Man'

stops.name: Rome, the Conclusiones printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1486; the day is a placement, and the sources describe the location of Eucharius Silber's press as approximated
stops.campa: The nine hundred conclusions go through a Roman press in December, without a title, and are sent out to the universities of Italy. The book will become, by one account, the first printed book universally banned by the Church, with nearly every copy burned. Among its theses stand the claim that Aristotle and Plato never disagreed except in words, the claim that Kabbalah confirms Christianity, and some hundreds of propositions Pico advances on his own authority and no one else's.
stops.quote: There is no inquiry, natural or theological, where Aristotle and Plato don't agree in meaning and content (sensu et re) even though they seem to disagree in words (verbis).
stops.quote_source: Conclusiones (900 Theses), quoted secondhand in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'
suggested_refs: The Conclusiones nongentae, Rome, December 1486, printed without a title
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Rome, the oration written for a debate that will not happen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1486; the month and day are placements. The text was neither published nor titled by Pico in his lifetime
stops.campa: He writes an opening address for the disputation and gives it no title. In it God finishes making the world, finds nothing left over to give the last creature, and gives him instead no fixed place, no proper form, no function of his own, so that he may make himself into whatever he chooses, downward into a plant or upward into an angel. It is never delivered. It is not printed while he lives. His nephew prints it two years after the death and calls it the Oration on the Dignity of Man.
stops.quote: We have given you, O Adam, no visage proper to yourself, nor endowment properly your own, in order that whatever place, whatever form, whatever gifts you may, with premeditation, select, these same you may have and possess through your own judgement and decision.
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, English translation hosted at bactra.org/Mirandola/
suggested_refs: The untitled 1486 Oratio, retitled by the 1496 edition
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'Oration on the Dignity of Man'

stops.name: The Apostolic Palace, the commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1487; the day is unknown. Sources give the count as thirteen contested, distributed by one account as seven condemned and six suspect; the commission's own tally was not reachable
stops.campa: The debate is announced for the sixth of January. Innocent VIII stops it before it opens and appoints a commission of bishops and theologians to read the nine hundred instead. They find thirteen they cannot pass: by the account that distributes them, seven condemned outright and six left suspect. He is asked to submit. He does not submit. He sits down and writes a defense of all thirteen, which is the decision that turns a scholarly quarrel into a proceeding.
stops.quote: In part heretical, in part the flower of heresy; several are scandalous and offensive to pious ears...
stops.quote_source: Attributed to the bull of Innocent VIII condemning the 900 Theses, 1487; not verified against the Latin text or any scholarly edition
suggested_refs: The commission of 1487 and its examination of the nine hundred conclusions
sources: Wikipedia (EN), 'Oration on the Dignity of Man'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Naples, the Apologia printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 31 May 1487; the Stanford Encyclopedia places the printing at Naples, and the research pool's Rome placement is an error. English Wikipedia's 1489 is an outlier and is not followed
stops.campa: The Apologia comes off a Neapolitan press at the end of May, defending every one of the thirteen and conceding nothing. He has answered a commission of the Roman Church as though it were an opposing party in a disputation, which is exactly what he believes it to be. Rome reads it as contumacy. The distinction between arguing a proposition and holding it, on which his whole enterprise rests, is the distinction the Curia declines to grant him. He is twenty-four years old.
suggested_refs: The Apologia of 31 May 1487, printed at Naples
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Rome, the bull and the order for his arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 August 1487
stops.campa: On the fourth of August the pope condemns the entire set of nine hundred, not the thirteen only, and orders the author taken. Copies are burned. Possession is forbidden. The young man who had offered to pay the fares of anyone willing to argue with him is now a fugitive with a papal warrant behind him. The philosophy meant to reconcile every school on earth has produced, as its first effect, a manhunt. He is a prince of Mirandola with nowhere in Italy to stand.
suggested_refs: The bull of Innocent VIII, 4 August 1487, condemning all nine hundred theses

segments.name: Flight, Arrest, and the King's Word

stops.name: North through Italy, the road to France
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted details the route; this pin stands for a road rather than an attested stop, and the month is a placement
stops.campa: He moves north out of Italy ahead of the officers, through territories where a papal warrant is honored to different degrees by different lords, aiming at France and the protection of a king. No source consulted follows him step by step. What is certain is that he crosses out of the peninsula in the last months of the year, alone or nearly so, carrying a condemned book that half the presses of Italy are under orders to destroy. He has been a fugitive for four months, and the record loses him for most of them.
suggested_refs: The Ligurian and Alpine routes out of Italy toward the French court, 1487
sources: Reconstructed from the general narrative of the flight in Britannica and Wikipedia, neither of which details the route

stops.name: Lyon, taken by the Duke of Savoy's officers
stops.date_confidence: attested to early 1488; sources place the arrest in the Lyon and Savoy region without agreeing on the exact spot, and the month and day are placements
stops.campa: Officers acting for Philip of Savoy, at the pope's request, seize him on French soil short of Paris. He has crossed a border and a mountain range and it has made no difference: the authority that wants him does not stop at frontiers. He is taken under guard toward the capital he had studied in three years before, this time as a prisoner of the Church in the keeping of a French duke. The sources put the seizure in the Lyon and Savoy country without agreeing on the spot. He has been at liberty for five months.
suggested_refs: The arrest of Pico by Savoyard officers in the Lyon region, 1488
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Vincennes, the fortress
stops.date_confidence: the imprisonment in France is attested; Vincennes specifically rests on Wikipedia and on tradition, and Britannica confirms the detention without naming a place. Month and day are placements
stops.campa: Tradition shuts him in the royal keep at Vincennes east of Paris, the tallest fortified tower in Europe, built to hold kings and used to hold whoever the crown found inconvenient. Britannica confirms a French prison and declines to name it. He is there weeks, not years. Across Italy the letters are already moving: Lorenzo de' Medici, other princes, a correspondence conducted with a French king about a young man they have decided is theirs and not the pope's.
suggested_refs: The donjon of the Chateau de Vincennes, named by tradition as the place of his confinement
sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola' (detention confirmed, place unnamed)

stops.name: Paris, freed by Charles VIII
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1488; the month is a placement
stops.campa: Charles VIII orders him released. Italian princes have petitioned, Lorenzo hardest of all, and the king of France has no interest in holding a scholar for the convenience of the Roman Curia. The condemnation is not lifted; nothing is retracted; he simply walks out and goes home. It is the second time Lorenzo's word has taken him out of custody in two years. He is never asked to repay it, and in April 1492 Lorenzo dies and the account closes itself.
suggested_refs: The intervention of Charles VIII and the Italian princes, 1488
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, home under Medici protection
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1488; the month is a placement within that season
stops.campa: He comes back to Tuscany as Lorenzo's guest and Lorenzo's charge. The papal sentence still stands, and nothing but Lorenzo's household stands against it. Pico is twenty-five, condemned in every particular by the head of his church, and living in the household of the most powerful private citizen in Europe. He does not stop writing. He stops, for the moment, printing anything he has not first put in front of Lorenzo, and he does not go to Rome again until Rome has changed popes.
suggested_refs: Lorenzo de' Medici's protection of a condemned man, 1488-1492
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Fiesole, the villa above Florence
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1489 for the settling; the research pool's geography lens gives a 1488-1492 span for the residence. Month unknown
stops.campa: Lorenzo prepares a villa for him at Fiesole on the hill above the city, and for four years this is where the work happens. Ficino is nearby. Poliziano is nearer. Below them Florence goes on banking for half of Europe and quarrelling with itself. It is the only settled stretch of his adult life. It runs from his twenty-sixth year to his twenty-ninth, and it ends in the week Lorenzo de' Medici dies at Careggi. The Heptaplus is written on this hill, and so is De ente et uno, and neither of them is the book Rome wanted burned.
suggested_refs: The Medici villa at Fiesole, prepared for Pico by Lorenzo

stops.name: Florence, the Heptaplus
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1489; the month is a placement. The papal tribunal and act of submission recorded under the same year rest on a single source and are carried as reconstruction
stops.campa: He publishes the Heptaplus, seven readings of the first twenty-six verses of Genesis, dedicated to Lorenzo. The method is the one the Theses were condemned for, applied where nobody could object: one text, read on seven levels at once, each level true, none of them cancelling another. It is a defense conducted as an exercise. By one account a papal tribunal opens against him in the same year, and he makes a formal act of submission to the propositions already condemned.
stops.quote: I have never philosophized save for the sake of philosophy, nor have I ever desired or hoped to secure from my studies and my laborious researches any profit or fruit save cultivation of mind and knowledge of the truth
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, English translation hosted at bactra.org/Mirandola/
suggested_refs: The Heptaplus, 1489, dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Reggio Emilia, hearing Savonarola dispute
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and the date is the weakest in this file. Wikipedia records the Reggio Emilia disputation at which Pico heard Savonarola but gives no year for it; the encounter is conventionally placed at the 1482 chapter. The 1490 stamp carried by the research pool belongs to Savonarola's recall to Florence, not to this meeting
stops.campa: At a Dominican chapter at Reggio Emilia he hears a friar named Girolamo Savonarola dispute, and is struck: not by eloquence, which the man then lacks, but by learning and by an austerity Pico has no equivalent for in himself. No source consulted fixes the year of that hearing. What the sources do fix is the consequence. Pico presses Lorenzo de' Medici to have the friar brought to Florence, and Lorenzo obliges him. The friar is a Ferrarese, and Pico had seen him once before, a decade earlier, in his own city.
suggested_refs: The Dominican chapter at Reggio Emilia, undated in the sources, at which Pico first heard Savonarola dispute

stops.name: San Marco, Savonarola brought to Florence
stops.date_confidence: attested to May or June 1490 for the arrival at San Marco
stops.campa: Savonarola comes to the convent of San Marco in the early summer, on Pico's advocacy and Lorenzo's order, and begins to preach. Within two years he is the loudest voice in Florence and within four he governs it in all but name. Pico is drawn to him steadily and then completely. The philosopher who wrote that a man may make himself into anything hands himself over to a friar who teaches that a man's business is to unmake himself. He will be buried under this floor.
suggested_refs: The convent of San Marco, Florence, and Savonarola's arrival there in 1490

stops.name: Mirandola, the estates handed to his nephew
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1491 by the Stanford Encyclopedia; month unknown. The research pool also carried 1489 for this act, and separately a record settling the inheritance on 'his two brothers' in 1482-1484, which contradicts both. Not resolved here; SEP is followed
stops.campa: He signs the family estates and the title over to his nephew Gianfrancesco Pico, keeping an income and keeping nothing else. The princedom of Mirandola, held by his house against Este and Gonzaga for generations, ceases to be his problem. Gianfrancesco will spend the rest of his own life editing, defending, and quietly reshaping his uncle's memory, and it is from Gianfrancesco's edition that Europe will learn what the Oration was called. Gianfrancesco also writes the life of his uncle that every later biographer starts from.
suggested_refs: The 1491 transfer of the Mirandola estates to Gianfrancesco Pico
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, De ente et uno written and not published
stops.date_confidence: the Stanford Encyclopedia dates the work after 1490 and states it remained unpublished in his lifetime; the research pool's '1491, publishes' is an error and is not followed. The month is a placement
stops.campa: He writes De ente et uno against Poliziano's Aristotelian objections, arguing that being and unity are one and the same, and that the Platonists and Aristotelians who have fought over the point for eighteen centuries have been fighting over a word. He does not print it. It stays in manuscript until his nephew gathers it into the posthumous collection. The reconciliation he was condemned for proposing to the world he now conducts privately, with one friend, in a room.
stops.quote: those who alienate Aristotle from Plato also alienate themselves from me, for I hold that their views are in harmony.
stops.quote_source: Conclusiones (900 Theses), quoted secondhand in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'
suggested_refs: De ente et uno, written after 1490, first printed in the 1496 Commentationes
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, the death of Lorenzo de' Medici
stops.date_confidence: the death is independently well documented to 8 or 9 April 1492; the summary source consulted for this record gives only the month
stops.campa: Lorenzo dies at Careggi in April and the protection dies with him. Nothing legal has changed: the condemnation of 1487 stands unrepealed, and the only thing that ever stood against it was one man's willingness to be inconvenient. Piero de' Medici succeeds his father and is not that man. Savonarola preaches. Charles VIII of France begins to look south at a peninsula with no arbiter left in it. Pico is twenty-nine and, for the first time since Arezzo, has nobody above him.
suggested_refs: The Medici villa at Careggi, where Lorenzo died in April 1492

stops.name: Ferrara, giving it away
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1492; the month is a placement
stops.campa: He moves to Ferrara for a period, still crossing back to Florence. He renounces his interest in the Egyptian and Chaldean books, burns his own vernacular love poetry, gives away money in quantities his household finds alarming, and lives thinner every year. The scholar who spent a fortune on Hebrew and Greek and Arabic manuscripts begins dismantling the life the library was for. Savonarola's letters follow him and he answers them the way a penitent answers a confessor.
suggested_refs: The destroyed vernacular poetry of Pico's Ferrara years

stops.name: The Apostolic Palace, absolved by Alexander VI
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1493; the research pool's June stamp is unsupported by any source consulted, and the month and day here are placements with no evidentiary value
stops.campa: Alexander VI, a Borgia with other priorities, absolves him of everything Innocent VIII condemned. Six years of standing outside the Church end with a document. It arrives when he has largely stopped wanting what it restores: the right to argue in public, the standing to summon Europe to a disputation. He is thirty. He is giving his property away and speaking of taking the Dominican habit, and he prints nothing more in the eighteen months he has left.
suggested_refs: The 1493 absolution granted by Alexander VI
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, the war on the astrologers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1493 for the beginning of the work, which was left unfinished; the month is a placement
stops.campa: He begins the Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem, twelve books demolishing judicial astrology: the stars act on bodies by light and heat and act on nothing else, and every prediction drawn from a nativity is a fraud on the will. The man who defended magic and Kabbalah in Rome takes apart the one occult science every court in Europe actually pays for. He does not finish it. Gianfrancesco publishes it after his death, and Kepler is still answering it a century on.
suggested_refs: Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem, begun 1493, unfinished at his death
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: Florence, death at thirty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to 17 November 1494; no source consulted fixes the house, and this pin is the city, not a residence
stops.campa: He dies on the seventeenth of November, thirty-one years old, in the hours when Charles VIII of France is entering Florence at the head of an army. Poliziano has died shortly before him. Contemporaries said poison and named his own secretary; a second rumor named Piero de' Medici, who is said to have feared what Pico and Savonarola were together. Nothing was proved in 1494. He had told Savonarola he meant to take the habit, and he is dressed in it for burial.
stops.quote: Our dear Pico left us on the same day that Charles VIII was entering Florence, and the tears of men of letters compensated for the joy of the people.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to a letter of Marsilio Ficino; carried by Wikipedia and not verified against a published edition of Ficino's correspondence
suggested_refs: The entry of Charles VIII into Florence, 17 November 1494
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giovanni Pico della Mirandola'

stops.name: San Marco, the friar speaks over him
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1494; the day is a placement
stops.campa: He is buried in the Dominican ground at San Marco, beside Girolamo Benivieni, who asks to be laid there with him and who composes the epitaph on the tomb. Savonarola preaches the funeral oration. Four years later that same friar is hanged and burned in the Piazza della Signoria half a mile from this floor, and the convent that received the philosopher is stormed by the city that had obeyed him. Angelo Poliziano lies here as well, dead two months before his friend. The three graves will be lost, and found again in 1933.
suggested_refs: The tomb at San Marco, Florence, with the epitaph attributed to Girolamo Benivieni

stops.name: Bologna, the Commentationes and a title
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1496 at Bologna per the Stanford Encyclopedia; month unknown. The research pool gave the place as the Duchy of Mirandola, taken from an infobox publication field and anachronistic besides, since Mirandola was not raised to a duchy until 1617
stops.campa: Gianfrancesco Pico gathers his uncle's papers and prints them at Bologna two years after the death. Among them is the untitled address written for the disputation that never opened, which this edition calls Oratio de hominis dignitate. The speech nobody heard becomes, under a title its author never gave it, the one text by which the Renaissance is taught to describe itself. What Pico published while alive is read today mainly by specialists in the field he made.
stops.quote: There is nothing to see more wonderful than man!
stops.quote_source: Oration on the Dignity of Man, trans. Richard Hooker, Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University
suggested_refs: The Commentationes of 1496, edited by Gianfrancesco Pico, first printing of the Oratio

stops.name: Basel, the Opera omnia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1601; month unknown
stops.campa: Sebastianus Henricpetri prints the complete works at Basel, a Protestant city, a hundred and seven years after the death. The condemned book travels north and keeps traveling; Giordano Bruno had gone the same way, looking for German presses that would take what Italy would not. Giulio Camillo had already built a wooden theatre of the Sephirot on this foundation and been called, when he died, a second Pico della Mirandola. Christian Kabbalah, which Pico named and programmed, is by now a discipline in the Empire with Johannes Reuchlin behind it.
suggested_refs: The Basel Opera omnia of 1601, printed by Sebastianus Henricpetri

stops.name: London, Walter Pater makes him a Renaissance
stops.date_confidence: the book is attested to 1873; the source gives only England as the place, and this pin is its place of publication rather than a documented location
stops.campa: Macmillan publishes Studies in the History of the Renaissance, and Walter Pater gives Pico a chapter. It is the chapter that fixes him in the modern imagination: the beautiful young prince who knew everything and died at thirty-one, the Renaissance itself in one body. Pater is not writing history and does not claim to be. In the same city, half a century on, Arthur Edward Waite reads Kabbalah under the dome of the British Museum and sets down what the Renaissance magicians took out of the Zohar and how much of it they got wrong in the taking.
suggested_refs: Walter Pater, Studies in the History of the Renaissance (Macmillan, 1873), chapter on Pico

stops.name: San Marco, the bones found again
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1933; month unknown
stops.campa: Father Vincenzo Chiaroni, searching the convent ground, finds the remains, and finds them where the sources said they would be: Pico, Poliziano, and Benivieni together. The three men who worked in the same rooms in the 1480s and died within four years of one another are still lying as they were put. Chiaroni records the identification and the graves are then left alone for seventy-four years. Nothing is taken from them and nothing is tested. The rumor of 1494 is still only a rumor.
suggested_refs: Vincenzo Chiaroni's 1933 rediscovery of the graves at San Marco

stops.name: Florence, the graves opened
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2007 for the exhumation; the month is a placement. Preliminary results were reported in 2008, and English Wikipedia records that the result for Poliziano was called inconclusive
stops.campa: The bodies of Pico and Poliziano are exhumed for forensic examination, five hundred and thirteen years after the burial. Preliminary results reported the following year point to arsenic in Pico; the result for Poliziano is called inconclusive. The rumor written down in 1494 and repeated as gossip for five centuries becomes, for the first time, a question that instruments can be pointed at. A second study eleven years later will report the same finding, and the sources do not agree on which of the two settled it.
suggested_refs: The 2007 exhumation of Pico and Poliziano and its preliminary 2008 report

stops.name: Mirandola, the castle shut
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 May 2012 for the collapse of the church of St Francis; the castle's closure dates from the same earthquake sequence. English Wikipedia's statement that the castle is open to the public predates 2012 and is stale
stops.campa: The second shock of the Emilia earthquake brings down the Gothic church of St Francis at Mirandola, which held the tombs of the Pico. The castle he was born in, restored and reopened to visitors in 2006, is left unusable: damage above ten million euros, the coins and maps carried to a bank vault in Modena, the paintings to Sassuolo. It stands under restoration still. The Palazzo del Comune of 1468, across the square, keeps its portraits of the family.
suggested_refs: The Castello dei Pico after the Emilia earthquake of May 2012, closed and under restoration

stops.name: Florence, arsenic confirmed
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 2018 by the Italian record; the day is unknown. The 2007 and 2018 rounds are kept as separate stops because the sources do not agree on which is decisive
stops.campa: Five hundred and twenty-four years after the death, a coordinated study by the biology department of the University of Pisa, the Carabinieri scientific investigation unit at Parma, and Spanish, British and German scholars reports that Pico was poisoned with arsenic. It names no hand. The Florentines who said the secretary, and the ones who said Piero de' Medici, are neither confirmed nor cleared by it. What is settled is only that they had been right about the manner of it.
suggested_refs: The November 2018 study by the University of Pisa and the Carabinieri RIS of Parma
